title: On‑call priority pathways and comm scripting
author: Marcus Liang
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines the priority pathways we use for oncall triage at Redwood Inference, standardized responder roles, and the customer/customer-facing comm templates we publish to the status page and to customers during incidents. It is intended for first responders, bridge operators, support engineers, and SREs who will own incident runloops and communications.

Scope:
- Applies to all production service incidents affecting hosted API, Dedicated, and Private control plane availability and correctness.
- Does NOT replace service-specific runbooks for deep technical remediation; rather it defines the operational flow, who talks to customers, and what we publish.

Goals and design principles:
1) Fast, consistent triage: reduce noisy escalations by following priority ladders.
2) Clear, empathetic customer comms with minimal technical jargon.
3) Explicit owner handoffs: every incident should have a single bridge operator and a named technical lead.
4) Playbooks that support graceful degradation and staged rollbacks.

Priority classification (high level):
1. P0 — Total outage or severe SLO breach impacting >10% of requests or any enterprise SLA trigger. Immediate bridge.
2. P1 — Major degradation (latency or error rate spike) affecting a subset of customers or paths (>1% of requests) with potential customer-impacting regressions. Time to initial response: 15 minutes.
3. P2 — Functional regressions with workarounds available or single-tenant impact without SLA triggers.
4. P3 — Informational alerts, low-impact errors, telemetry noise, or follow-up items scheduled for normal cycles.

SLO & alert thresholds (examples):
- API availability SLO: 99.95% regionally over 30d.
- Latency P1 trigger: 90th percentile generation latency > 2x baseline for 30 minutes.
- Error rate P0 trigger: 5xx rate > 3% of requests for 10 minutes and customer-visible failures reported.

Responder roles and responsibilities:
- Bridge Operator (BO): owns the incident timeline, customer-facing status updates, and coordinates handoffs.
- First Responder (FR): performs immediate triage steps, collects logs, reproducer (if possible), and executes containment actions from the runbook.
- Service Lead / Technical Lead (TL): deep debugging, changelist/fix decisions, and rollback authority.
- Customer Success Liaison (CSL): translates technical status to commercial stakeholders for enterprise customers and leads case-specific comms.
- Incident Commander (IC): invoked for P0s or escalations; makes the call for postmortem and resource allocation.

Triage decision ladder (quick checklist for FR):
1) Acknowledge alert and join the incident channel (Slack/bridge) within the SLA window.
2) Confirm scope and blast radius: region(s), model(s), routes, customer tiers affected.
3) Check upstream/infra signals: GPU hosts, autoscaling, K8s node events, network errors.
4) Attempt containment: circuit breakers, throttle policy, route to fallback model variant.
5) If containment succeeds, coordinate controlled roll-forward or canary. If not, escalate to TL + IC for P0.

Runbook snippet: KV cache surge (example common for serving runtime)
- Trigger: sudden increase in CPU on KV cache host, resulting in token generation stalls and 502 responses.
- Immediate actions (FR):
  1. Mark service route as degraded in feature toggle to stop new long-running requests.
  2. Clear ephemeral KV cache for affected host: curl -XPOST https://infra-api.internal/cache/flush?host=<host-id> (use runbook token).
  3. If hosts are under autoscaling, check ASG metrics and open capacity breach alarms.
  4. If traffic redistribution is needed, update routing to use region fallback: rcli route apply --policy fallback:nearby.
- Escalation: If error rates remain >2% after 10 minutes, escalate to TL.
- Recovery verification: 99% of requests successful and 95th percentile latency < baseline*1.5 for 10 consecutive minutes.

Escalation matrix (simplified):
- FR -> BO after 10 minutes if no containment.
- BO -> TL for technical escalation.
- TL -> IC for P0 decision or customer-exposed SLA action.
- BO -> CSL to prepare enterprise comms once blast radius confirmed.

Customer-facing communications (templates)
- Public status page template (short):
  Title: Degraded generation performance in us-west-2
  Summary: We are investigating increased latency for model generation in the us-west-2 region. Some customers may experience delayed responses or timeouts.
  Impact: Partial regional degradation affecting ~18% of requests to us-west-2.
  Next update: 30 minutes or earlier.
  Mitigation: Traffic is being diverted to nearby regions and fallback models where compatible.
  Owner: Incident bridge (link to bridge).

- Escalated public status page (when fix deployed):
  Title: Restoration in progress — us-west-2
  Summary: A mitigation has been deployed that is restoring normal throughput. Latency is trending down; we will confirm recovery metrics and close the incident once SLO criteria are met.
  Impact: Partial impact remains for sessions with >8k token prefixes until cache repopulation completes.
  Next update: 1 hour.
  Owner: Incident bridge.

- Enterprise customer email/CS template (example):
  Subject: Incident update — Degraded response times in us‑west‑2 (Incident #12345)
  Body:
  Hello <Customer Name>,

  We wanted to inform you of an ongoing incident affecting generation latency for the us-west-2 region. Our engineering team has identified high KV cache contention on a subset of hosts as the root cause. We have deployed traffic diversion to nearby pools and a targeted cache flush. Some sessions with long context windows may still see slower responses while caches repopulate.

  Current status: Mitigation in progress; overall request success rate improved from 72% to 94% in the last 15 minutes.
  ETA for full recovery: 60–90 minutes.
  Actions taken: Traffic diversion, cache flush, autoscaling of affected pools.
  Contact: Your Customer Success manager (cc'd) and incident bridge: <bridge link>.

  We will follow up with a detailed post-incident report.

  Thanks,
  Redwood Inference Incident Team

Internal comm cadence and timing rules:
- First internal bridge update: within 15 minutes of incident creation for P0/P1.
- Public status page first post: within 30 minutes for any incident with user-visible impact.
- Enterprise direct outreach: within 60 minutes for customers affected at SLA thresholds.
- Update cadence: every 30 minutes until containment, then hourly until recovery verification.

Hand-offs, rotation notes, and oncall progression:
- Handover checklist for outgoing oncall (5–15 minutes before rotation end):
  - Verify bridge owner recorded in channel and update the incident ticker.
  - List current mitigations, in-flight actions, and outstanding TL tasks.
  - Confirm customer comms and next update ETA.
  - Ensure runbook tokens and credentials are rotated if used for mitigation (see secure operations).
- Rotation progression: new oncall reviews active incidents for 10 minutes, confirms understanding, and then accepts ownership in bridge. If unclear, escalate to the original BO for a 10-minute shadow.

Game day playbook (quarterly simulation):
1) Purpose: validate triage ladder, BO/FR/TL interactions, status page workflow, and customer outreach templates.
2) Frequency: quarterly for SRE and product infra teams; additional tenant-focused game days annually with CS.
3) Scenario example: forced KV eviction and throttling in a single region during peak traffic.
4) Measured metrics: time-to-ack, time-to-containment, time-to-first-public-update, accuracy of comm templates, and postmortem action closure rate.
5) After-action deliverables: a retro with action owners and scheduled fixes (within 2 weeks of exercise).

Postmortem template (required for P0/P1 where there is material customer impact):
- Title: "<Short descriptive name> — Incident #<id>"
- Summary: one-paragraph incident narrative
- Timeline: minute-level chronology with person on-call, bridge link, and commands executed
- Root cause: succinct technical root cause and contributing factors
- Customer impact: metrics (requests failed, customers affected, SLA exposure)
- Mitigation and recovery steps taken
- Follow-up actions (owner, ETA, priority)
- Detection gaps and monitoring improvements
- Communication timeline and external messaging review

Runbook governance and testing:
- Every runbook must be reviewed annually and after any postmortem that used it.
- Runbooks that are executed in production need a certified runner (FR or TL) to sign off in the postmortem.
- CLI/automation snippets must exist in the infra repo with pinned version tags; link snippets in the runbook to avoid drift.

Security and sensitive ops notes:
- Do NOT include secrets, service tokens, or raw enterprise customer identifiers in public status page entries. Use ticket IDs and anonymized metrics instead.
- For Private deployments, coordinate with the customer's security contact before publishing technical details that reference on-prem host identifiers.

Appendix: useful commands and dashboards
- Quick queries:
  - Check error rate by route: curl -s "https://metrics-api.internal/query?m=error_rate&route=<route>"
  - Retrieve recent 500s: rcli logs tail --service=model-serving --filter "status>=500" --since 15m
- Dashboards to review on triage:
  - Serving: Production Latency (region), Request Error Heatmap, KV cache hit ratio
  - Infra: GPU host CPU/Memory, Node Reboots, Autoscaler activity
